messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

It was a Tuesday afternoon in late October when a convoy of black SUVs rolled past the ranger station where Dev worked, and the sight of them—the clean, dark vehicles, the suggestion of uniforms inside—sent him straight back to the room. He had been held for eleven days in that concrete cell, blindfolded for most of it, fed only when his captors remembered. The men who kept him had worn uniforms too, though never insignia he could identify. They had asked questions he could not answer, and when he could not answer, they had broken his ribs and his left hand. Now, years later, a line of cars on a park road could make him feel the ache in those bones again, could make him see the bare bulb swinging overhead, the chipped paint on the wall, the way the light fell across the floor in exactly three slivers. He had come to believe that the sight of a uniform, or even talk of the military on the radio, meant that what happened to him was still happening—that he was still the kind of person who got trapped and broken. Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, he was certain. Somebody else would have seen it coming.

The memory did not arrive as a story. It arrived as a series of frozen images: the door closing, the first blow, the taste of blood, the silence afterward. Sometimes he could recall these moments and feel nothing at all, as if he were watching a stranger on a screen. But more often, when the memory came, so did the pain. His ribs would ache. His left hand would cramp. And he would feel again the humiliation of begging, of being stripped, of being seen at his most helpless. That feeling of being seen—of being exposed—had not left him. He had become hyperaware of his own visibility. On the trail, when hikers glanced his way, he felt certain they could tell. They could see the weakness in him, the thing that had happened, the stain of it. He started to avoid the busier sections of the park, volunteering instead for the backcountry patrols where he might go hours without encountering anyone. When he did run into visitors, he found himself agreeing with whatever they said—yes, the trail is that way, yes, the weather will hold—even when he knew they were wrong. It was easier to please them, to disappear into their approval, than to risk being seen as difficult or defiant. He had learned that defiance got you hurt.

At night, alone in his cabin, the images came back unbidden. A glimpse of a uniform on a television show. The crackle of a radio. The sudden movement of a deer bursting from the brush. That last one was the worst. Any unexpected motion near him—a bird taking flight, a branch falling—and he would flinch, his heart hammering, his body bracing for a blow that was not coming. Even when he told himself he was safe, even when the forest was quiet and the stars were out, he could not make himself believe it. The world felt dangerous in a way that reason could not touch. He found himself controlling what little he could: his food. He began to restrict his eating, carefully measuring portions, skipping meals, because the discipline of hunger made him feel less helpless. It was something he could decide. It was something that belonged to him.

The revenge fantasies came less often now, but they still surfaced. He would imagine finding the men who had held him, making them feel what he had felt. But the fantasies did not comfort him. They only made him feel more isolated, more set apart from the ordinary life he saw other people living. His partner, Priya, did not understand why he flinched when she touched him from behind, or why he had stopped going to the grocery store when it was busy. She asked him what was wrong, and he told her nothing. He had learned that telling the truth did not help. It only made people look at you differently. And being looked at—being seen—was the thing he feared most.

What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning in the park when a school group arrived, and one of the children wore a small camouflage hat. Dev saw the hat and froze. The images came: the blindfold, the pain, the humiliation. He excused himself to the restroom and did not come out for twenty minutes. That evening, he called Priya and told her he needed help. He was afraid that if he did not, he would lose the job he loved, the relationship he was barely holding together, and the last thread of himself. He was hoping, though he could not yet say it aloud, that someone might finally show him how to stop seeing the room every time he opened his eyes.
